subject: AIC got worse with MLM estimator

messages.author: b48ebf16ed4cffef
messages.subject: AIC got worse with MLM estimator
parts:
Hi can someone explain to me why and how I can fix this problem? I fitted two SEM models using maximum likelihood estimation with robust standard errors and Satorra-Bentler Chi-square test statistic. The M00.robust is my saturated model and M01.robust, my first unsatured one.  and compared them using AIC. However, when I remove the first variable from this unsatured model the AIC got worse. I don't know how to fix this. I read in somewhere that Mplus provides correct nested tests for robust methods, but I didn't find any info about how one can do it in Lavaan. I appreciate any help in this regard.

AIC(M01.robust, M00.robust)
                            df       AIC
M01.robust    27   -58.93755
M00.robust    28   -56.97216

Thank you again for helping me.

messages.author: 12fdd832cacb825e
messages.subject: Re: AIC got worse with MLM estimator
parts:
VInicius,

When you say you "removed a variable," do you mean you took it out of
the analysis completely? The statistics aren't going to be comparable
in that case, because they depend on the original variance/covariance
matrix, which is going to compose different data in the two models.

With the same data, changing the model can move the AIC in either
direction, as it includes an adjustment for the number of parameters
estimated.

Pat

messages.author: 12fdd832cacb825e
messages.subject: Re: AIC got worse with MLM estimator
parts:
Generally, the difference test is preferred when the models being
compared are nested because its properties are well established. Note
that it does assume that the full (less-restricted) fits well,
generally interpreted as non-significant chi-squared. AIC and related
approaches (BIC, adjBIC) are more often used when the models being
compared are not nested, because the difference test does not apply to
that situation.

parts: Thank you so much for your help. 🙏
Em seg, 11 de jan de 2021 14:00, Patrick (Malone Quantitative) <mal...@malonequantitative.com> escreveu:

Generally, the difference test is preferred when the models being
compared are nested because its properties are well established. Note
that it does assume that the full (less-restricted) fits well,
generally interpreted as non-significant chi-squared. AIC and related
approaches (BIC, adjBIC) are more often used when the models being
compared are not nested, because the difference test does not apply to
that situation.

On Mon, Jan 11, 2021 at 11:55 AM Vinicius Alvarenga
<vinicius.s...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Oh, mate, thank you so much! You're completely right about that; the AIC improved sightly from M00 to M01. I hadn't noticed that because of the magnitude of the negative sign. Any way, for AIC scores lower is better, isn't it? In relation to your question, I get confused when to use one [AIC]  or another [LRT] test. What should one do when the LRT test between two models isn't significant? Alternatively, what happens when it is significant? Should I accept the more restricted or the less restricted model? Thank you.
>
> Em seg., 11 de jan. de 2021 às 13:20, Patrick (Malone Quantitative) <mal...@malonequantitative.com> escreveu:
>>
>> Also, note that AIC appears to have improved from M00 to M01. Lower is better.
>>
>> On Mon, Jan 11, 2021 at 11:19 AM Patrick (Malone Quantitative)
>> <mal...@malonequantitative.com> wrote:
>> >
>> > Is there any particular reason you're relying on AIC instead of a
>> > (scaled) difference test?
>> >
>> > On Mon, Jan 11, 2021 at 8:31 AM Vinicius Alvarenga
>> > <vinicius.s...@gmail.com> wrote:
>> > >
>> > > Sorry about that, Patrick. Instead of removing a "variable" as a whole, I meant a path from an exogenous variable to another endogenous one. I wanted to do this process iteratively, but as the AIC already got worse in the first round, I do not know what to do. Do you have any idea?
>> > >
>> > > Thank you.
>> > >
>> > > Em seg., 11 de jan. de 2021 às 10:17, Patrick (Malone Quantitative) <mal...@malonequantitative.com> escreveu:
>> > >>
>> > >> VInicius,
>> > >>
>> > >> When you say you "removed a variable," do you mean you took it out of
>> > >> the analysis completely? The statistics aren't going to be comparable
>> > >> in that case, because they depend on the original variance/covariance
>> > >> matrix, which is going to compose different data in the two models.
>> > >>
>> > >> With the same data, changing the model can move the AIC in either
>> > >> direction, as it includes an adjustment for the number of parameters
>> > >> estimated.
>> > >>
>> > >> Pat
>> > >>
>> > >> On Mon, Jan 11, 2021 at 8:04 AM Vinicius Alvarenga
>> > >> <vinicius.s...@gmail.com> wrote:
>> > >> >
>> > >> > Hi can someone explain to me why and how I can fix this problem? I fitted two SEM models using maximum likelihood estimation with robust standard errors and Satorra-Bentler Chi-square test statistic. The M00.robust is my saturated model and M01.robust, my first unsatured one.  and compared them using AIC. However, when I remove the first variable from this unsatured model the AIC got worse. I don't know how to fix this. I read in somewhere that Mplus provides correct nested tests for robust methods, but I didn't find any info about how one can do it in Lavaan. I appreciate any help in this regard.
